190.title: Pauri 18: countless fools
190.hook: asankh moorakh: countless fools, thieves and liars too, and Nanak calls himself lowly (Japji 18)
190.howItsDone: Pauri 18 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs point to its closing line, in which Guru Nanak calls himself lowly, as a model of humility.

segments.voice: Yesterday, asankh, countless: countless devotions, none ranked. Your line was countless, and good. Today, the same word turns around and looks at the other side.

You know the feeling of reading the news and thinking: people are idiots. The driver who cut you off. The scammer. The politician caught lying. Somebody's comment under a video. It's easy, and weirdly satisfying, to make a list of everyone who's wrong. Pauri 18 makes that list. It's long, and it's harsh. And at the very end, the one making the list does something almost nobody does after a list like that. He puts himself on it.
screen: `PEOPLE ARE IDIOTS.` → `A LIST OF EVERYONE WHO'S WRONG.` → `HE PUTS HIMSELF ON IT.`

segments.voice: Pauri 17 counted the countless devoted. Pauri 18 counts the countless who've gone wrong, and it opens: asankh moorakh andh ghor. Countless fools, blind in deep darkness. Then, in paraphrase: countless thieves, and people who live off what isn't theirs. Countless who rule by force and then are gone. Countless who cut throats and kill. Countless who do wrong and keep doing it. Countless liars, wandering in their lies. Countless slanderers, carrying the weight of it on their heads. It doesn't soften anything. Creation includes all of this, and it's countless too. Then the last line, in the original: naanak neech kahai veechaar. Nanak, the lowly, offers this reflection. Neech means low, lowly. Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh path, closes a list of fools and thieves by calling himself low. Commentators read it a few ways. Some hear pure humility: the one who speaks is no higher than anyone he's described. Some hear something sharper: the speaker won't pretend he's outside the list. Either way, it takes the sting of superiority out of the whole stanza. Then the refrain: I can't even once be a sacrifice to You. Whatever pleases You is good. You are forever safe, Formless One. So the countless include the saints and the scoundrels, and the voice that names them stands low, among them, not above.
screen: `ASANKH MOORAKH — COUNTLESS FOOLS.` · `THIEVES, TYRANTS, LIARS, SLANDERERS.` · `NAANAK NEECH KAHAI VEECHAAR.` · `LOW, AMONG THEM, NOT ABOVE.` · then, large: `NANAK THE LOWLY.`

segments.voice: Hold one opinion you feel strongly about other people, who's foolish, who's wrong, and ask: what if I'm missing something here? You don't have to drop it; just let it sit a little lower, a little less sure. If a need to be right comes up, notice it, and let it soften as you breathe.
Neech. Low, lowly: what Nanak calls himself, at the end of a pauri counting countless fools, thieves, tyrants and liars.
Your line: nanak the lowly. Humility, even at the end of a list of thieves and liars. That's day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Pauri 19, sound: asankh naav
191.howItsDone: Pauri 19 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; its opening line, asankh naav asankh thaav, is the last of the stanzas built on asankh, countless.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neech, the lowly, and countless fools, with Guru Nanak standing among them. Your line was nanak the lowly. Today, the last countless stanza begins.

Names for God, or for whatever people mean by the deepest thing, pile up fast. A grandmother uses one word, a friend another, an old hymn a third. One city street can hold them in several languages, whispered in kitchens and sung behind closed doors. Then there are the places people call holy: rivers, mountains, rooms, a spot under one particular tree. Pauri 19 starts right there, with names and places, and it says both are beyond counting.
screen: `SO MANY NAMES.` → `SO MANY HOLY PLACES.` → `BEYOND COUNTING, BOTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 19 in the original: asankh naav asankh thaav. Four words, two pairs. Asankh you know: countless. Naav, said NAAV, with a long a: names. It's a form of naam, the Name, a word at the center of Sikh life. Thaav, THAAV: places. Countless names, countless places. Hear the rhyme: naav, thaav, the second word landing right on top of the first. It's the third stanza in a row to lean on asankh. Pauri 17 counted devotions. Pauri 18 counted fools. Pauri 19 counts names and places, and then, in paraphrase, goes further: countless worlds, beyond reach, beyond reach. Then a twist. Even to say countless, it says, is to carry a weight on your head. Even the word asankh is too small. Three stanzas built on countless, and Guru Nanak admits that countless isn't big enough either. The same humility as yesterday, turned on language itself. Tomorrow, where the stanza goes next: to letters and words, and why it doesn't give up on them. Today, the sound. Asankh naav, asankh thaav. Said slowly, it opens like a wide room. Said quickly, it keeps time like a pulse. Anyone who recites Japji each morning meets it every day.
screen: `NAAV — NAMES. THAAV — PLACES.` · `NAAV, THAAV: ONE RHYME.` · `A THIRD STANZA OF COUNTLESS.` · `EVEN COUNTLESS IS TOO SMALL.` · then, large: `ASANKH NAAV.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud, asankh naav, asankh thaav: once slowly, feeling the rhyme land, then softer, then almost a whisper. Let it go silent and sit. If you like, let the words ride quietly on your breath, asankh naav on the in-breath, asankh thaav on the out-breath.
Thaav. Places: countless of them, asankh thaav, alongside asankh naav, countless names, and then even countless is called too small a word.
Your line: asankh naav. Countless names, countless places, and even countless too small a word. Until tomorrow.

192.title: Pauri 19, meaning: through letters
192.hook: countless names and places; yet through letters we speak the Name and sing His praise (Japji 19)
192.howItsDone: Pauri 19 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; learning the Gurmukhi letters, the painti akhar, is a first step toward reading Gurbani.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thaav, places, and the sound of Pauri 19. Your line was asankh naav: countless names, and even countless too small a word. Today, the stanza's surprise.

A child's name in giant wobbly letters, taped to a bedroom door. A small thing doing a big job. A few shapes of ink, and someone across the room, or across the world, or long after, can hear what was meant. Pauri 19 has just said even countless is too small a word for creation. You'd expect it to give up on words entirely. It doesn't. It turns and praises the smallest thing we have: the letter.
screen: `A NAME IN WOBBLY LETTERS.` → `A FEW SHAPES OF INK.` → `THE STANZA PRAISES THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Today's word is akhar: a letter, a written character. Here's the heart of the stanza in the original: akharee naam akharee saalaah. Through letters, the Name. Through letters, praise. Then, in paraphrase: through letters, knowledge and songs and the singing of virtues. Through letters, writing and speaking. Through letters, even what's written on each person's forehead, their destiny, is told. Everything we can say about the sacred comes through these little shapes and sounds. Then a turn: the One who wrote all this has nothing written on His own forehead. No one assigns the Writer a destiny. As He commands, so things are received. As much as He has made, so much is His Name. And without the Name, there is no place at all. So the stanza holds two things together. Words can never contain it. And yet words are how we reach toward it. That has a place in Sikh life. Sikh tradition credits the second Guru, Guru Angad, with shaping the Gurmukhi script, the letters the Guru Granth Sahib is written in. Learning those letters is a first step toward reading Gurbani. One more layer some readers point out: akhar is related to the Sanskrit akshara, a letter or a syllable, a word that can also mean imperishable. The letter that can't hold everything is also a thing that lasts. That closes the countless stanzas: countless devotions, countless fools, countless names. And through letters, the Name.
screen: `AKHAREE NAAM AKHAREE SAALAAH.` · `THE WRITER HAS NO FOREHEAD LINES.` · `SMALL, AND YET THE WAY IN.` · `AKSHARA — IMPERISHABLE.` · then, large: `THROUGH LETTERS, THE NAME.`

segments.voice: If you have paper or a phone nearby, write one word you love, a name, a place, a quality like kindness or home, slowly, one letter at a time; if you can't write right now, trace it with a finger on your knee. Look at the shapes and notice how much those few marks carry. Then sit with it, breathing.
Akhar. A letter. Through letters, Pauri 19 says, come the Name, praise, knowledge and song; related to the Sanskrit akshara, which can also mean imperishable.
Your line: through letters, the name. Small shapes, and yet the way in. Day one hundred ninety-two, done.

193.title: Pauri 20, sound: bhareeai hath
193.tomorrow: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind
193.howItsDone: Pauri 20 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; the Sikh code of conduct describes rising early, bathing, and then reciting Japji, so its opening picture of washing sits close to the morning itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akhar, the letter, and the end of the countless stanzas. Your line was through letters, the name. Today, Japji comes down to earth.

Muddy hands after gardening. Sticky hands after a mango. The feeling after a long day when your whole body just wants a shower. For four stanzas, Japji has been looking up and out: countless worlds, countless names, a bull holding up the earth. Now, suddenly, it looks down at your hands. It's about as ordinary as a picture gets, and Guru Nanak starts a new stanza with it. From the edge of the universe to the kitchen sink, in one breath.
screen: `MUDDY HANDS, STICKY HANDS.` → `AFTER COUNTLESS WORLDS, YOUR HANDS.` → `FROM THE UNIVERSE TO THE SINK.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 20 in the original: bhareeai hath pair tan deh. Word by word. Bhareeai, said BHA-ree-ai: when it's filled, when it's covered, when it's soiled. It's built on the everyday verb for filling, as you'd fill a glass; here it means covered in dirt. Hath: hands. Pair: feet. Tan and deh: two words for the body, one after the other, as if to say the whole body, all of it. So: when the hands, the feet, the whole body are covered in dirt. Hear the rhythm. Bhareeai, a long rolling word, then four short ones, hath, pair, tan, deh, like four quick splashes. The next line, in paraphrase, gives the answer everyone knows: pour on water, and the dust comes off. Nothing mysterious. Anyone who's ever washed their hands knows it. That's how the stanza begins, with something so obvious it almost doesn't need saying. And that's the teacher's trick. Start with what everybody already agrees on: hands get dirty; water cleans them. Then, once you're nodding, move to something you might not have thought about. Tomorrow we follow the stanza from the body to the mind, and see what it says washes that. Today, just the sound and the picture. Bhareeai hath: dirty hands.
screen: `BHAREEAI — FILLED, COVERED, SOILED.` · `HATH, PAIR, TAN, DEH.` · `WATER, AND THE DUST COMES OFF.` · `START WITH WHAT EVERYONE KNOWS.` · then, large: `BHAREEAI HATH.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud once slowly, bhareeai hath pair tan deh, then again, bringing your attention to each part as you name it: hands, feet, the whole body. Then rest your hands in your lap, palms up, and simply feel them: warm or cool, heavy or light.
Deh. The body: named alongside tan in this pauri's opening, bhareeai hath pair tan deh, when hands, feet and body are soiled, and water washes the dust away.
Your line: bhareeai hath. The body comes first in this stanza; the mind comes next. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 193 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 20, MEANING: WHAT WASHES THE MIND.`

194.title: Pauri 20, meaning: what washes the mind
194.hook: water washes dirty hands and soap soiled clothes; a mind soiled by wrong is dyed clean by love of the Name; as you sow, you reap (Japji 20)
194.howItsDone: Pauri 20 is recited in Japji Sahib each morning; Sikhs often speak of being dyed in the Name, rang, and quote aape beej aape hee khaahu to say that each person reaps what they sow.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deh, the body, and the sound of Pauri 20. Your line was bhareeai hath: dirty hands, and water to wash them. Today, where the stanza goes next.

Some stains come out with water. Some need soap and a good scrub. And some things a person did years ago sit on them like a stain no laundry will lift: a cruel word to a brother, a friend let down. A shower doesn't touch it; it's still there at two in the morning. Pauri 20 walks right up to that stain, one step at a time.
screen: `WATER FOR SOME STAINS.` → `SOAP FOR OTHERS.` → `AND THE STAIN AT 2AM?`

segments.voice: Pauri 20 climbs a little ladder. Step one, yesterday's: when hands, feet and body are dirty, water washes the dust off. Step two, in paraphrase: when clothes are soiled, even badly, you apply soap and wash them clean. Step three, and here the stanza turns: when the mind is soiled by wrongdoing, it is washed by the love of the Name. The original has a lovely word there: oh dhopai naavai kai rang. Rang is color, dye. The mind isn't only scrubbed; it's dyed, soaked through in the color of the Name, the way cloth takes on a new color in the vat. In Sikh writing, being dyed in the Name, rang, is a recurring picture of love that goes all the way through. Then the stanza keeps this from being too easy. Virtuous and sinner, it says, aren't just labels people say. What you do, again and again, is written down and goes with you. And the line behind today's carry, in the original: aape beej aape hee khaahu. You yourself sow, and you yourself eat. Whatever seed you plant is the harvest you'll live on. Nanak says we come and go by the Hukam, the divine order. So two things stand side by side. The Name can dye even a stained mind clean. And actions still matter; you eat what you plant. Grace and responsibility, in one stanza, and it doesn't let go of either.
screen: `WATER FOR HANDS, SOAP FOR CLOTHES.` · `THE MIND, DYED IN THE NAME.` · `LABELS AREN'T ENOUGH.` · `AAPE BEEJ AAPE HEE KHAAHU.` · then, large: `AS YOU SOW.`

segments.voice: If you can, wash your hands now, slowly, feeling the water, the soap, each finger; if you can't get to a sink, rub your palms together as if washing them. As you do, let one small thing you'd like to be washed clean of be there with the water, without dwelling on it. Then sit, hands resting, and breathe.
Rang. Color, dye: the mind soaked through in the color of the Name. Water washes hands, soap washes clothes, and the love of the Name dyes the mind clean. And you eat what you sow.
Your line: as you sow. The Name dyes the mind, and the harvest is still yours. That's day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: Pauri 21, sound: teerath tap
195.tomorrow: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
195.howItsDone: Pauri 21 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs give daswandh, a tenth of their earnings, and visit gurdwaras such as Harmandir Sahib, while hearing this stanza as a reminder that the inner change matters most.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rang, the mind dyed clean in the Name. Your line was as you sow. Today, a stanza that opens with five famous good deeds.

A checklist for being a good person. Go on the big trip to the holy place. Fast, or give something up. Be kind. Give to charity, and give generously. Most people would call that a solid list. Now imagine someone reading your list, nodding, and saying: those are good. And all together, they're worth about as much as a sesame seed, if what's inside you hasn't changed. Pauri 21 opens with that list, and its sound is worth learning first.
screen: `A CHECKLIST FOR BEING GOOD.` → `PILGRIMAGE, FASTING, KINDNESS, GIVING.` → `WORTH A SESAME SEED?`

segments.voice: Here is the opening line in the original: teerath tap daiaa dat daan. Five words, five practices. Teerath, TEE-rath: you know it from Pauri 6, the holy bathing place where Nanak said he'd bathe only if it pleased the One. There it stood alone; here it leads a whole line. Tap, TUP, rhymes with cup: austerity, self-discipline, the word's root meaning heat. Daiaa: compassion, which we met in the bull stanza. Dat and daan: gifts, giving, charity. Said aloud, it rolls like a list: teerath, tap, daiaa, dat, daan. The next line, in paraphrase: if anyone gains honor from these, it's only as much as a sesame seed. Til, the tiny seed. Not nothing. Just small. Now, careful here. The stanza isn't mocking pilgrims or givers, and Sikhs themselves give generously and visit holy places, Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar most of all. It's weighing where the real change happens. The next lines say where, in paraphrase: the one who has listened, has trusted, and has loved in the mind has bathed at the pilgrimage place within. Hear the words coming back? Listening, suniai. Trusting, mannai. And love. The words of Pauris 8 to 15 return all at once. The real teerath is inside. Teerath tap daiaa dat daan: five good things, honored, and pointed inward.
screen: `TEERATH — A FORD, A HOLY PLACE.` · `TAP, DAIAA, DAT, DAAN.` · `WORTH A SESAME SEED.` · `THE PILGRIMAGE PLACE WITHIN.` · then, large: `TEERATH TAP.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud slowly, teerath tap daiaa dat daan, five words like five steps, then twice more, and let it go quiet. Think of one good thing you did this week; don't grade it, just ask gently whether it moved anything inside you. Rest with whatever answer comes, breathing.
Teerath, the holy pilgrimage place. It opens teerath tap daiaa dat daan: pilgrimage, austerity, compassion, gifts and giving, and points to the pilgrimage place within.
Your line: teerath tap. The real pilgrimage place, the stanza says, is the one within. Day one hundred ninety-five, done.

196.title: Pauri 21, meaning: when was the world made
196.hook: no pandit, qazi or yogi knows the hour creation began; only the Creator knows (Japji 21)
196.howItsDone: Pauri 21 is recited each morning in Japji Sahib; Sikh commentary reads its lines on the pandits, qazis and yogis to say that the beginning of creation is known only to the Creator.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 21. Your line was teerath tap: five good deeds, and the pilgrimage place within. And that ends a week: Nanak the lowly among the fools he named, countless names, through letters the Name, dirty hands, as you sow.
screen: `TEERATH — TEERATH TAP.` → `THE WEEK: LOWLY, LETTERS, SOWING.`

segments.voice: A kid at the dinner table asks: when did the world start? What day? What time? The adults look at each other. Someone mentions the Big Bang. Someone else says it depends who you ask. Everybody's guessing. Pauri 21 asks that exact question, very precisely, and then gives an answer that's both humble and bold.
screen: `WHEN DID THE WORLD START?` → `WHAT DAY? WHAT TIME?` → `EVERYBODY'S GUESSING.`

segments.voice: Here's how the question is asked, in paraphrase. What was that moment, what was the hour? What lunar day, what day of the week? What season, what month, when the form of the world came to be? A birth certificate for the universe. Then Guru Nanak goes around the room of his day. The pandits, the Hindu scholars, didn't find the time; if they had, it would be written in the Puranas. The qazis, the Muslim judges and scholars, didn't find the moment; if they had, they would have written it in the Qur'an. The yogi doesn't know the day or the weekday. No one knows the season or the month. Then the answer, in the original: jaa kartaa sirathee kau saaje aape jaanai soee. The Maker who shaped creation, He alone knows. Notice how even-handed it is: pandits, qazis, yogis, the learned of the communities around Guru Nanak. It mocks none of them. It simply says: this is beyond all of us. The stanza goes on, in paraphrase: how can I speak of it, how praise it, how describe it, how know it? Everyone speaks, each trying to be wiser than the next. Great is the Master, great is His Name. And whoever thinks they're something on their own won't be honored in the end. So the lesson isn't anti-knowledge. Sikhs value learning; Japji itself is full of it. It's about the edge of knowledge, and the honesty to stand there and say: I don't know, and the Maker does.
